reconcile.connective: Defenders read God's order to Hosea not as a license to fornicate but either as a vision/enacted parable that never literally occurred, or as a marriage made lawful by the divine command itself.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells, who catalogues Hosea 1:2 as God ordering the prophet to take a "wife of whoredoms," i.e., commanding the very adultery his own law forbids.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013); skepticsannotatedbible.com

excerpts.excerpt_text: not that the Prophet did this thing in effect, but he saw this in a vision, or else was commanded by God to set forth under this parable or figure the idolatry of the Synagogue, and of the people her children.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the conflict: the command was not an actual act of taking a harlot but a vision/parable, so no real fornication was commanded.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The reference to the children of whoredom, along with the wife of whoredom, indicates unquestionably priori, that the divine command did not contemplate an actual and outward marriage, but simply a symbolical representation of the relation in which the idolatrous Israelites were then standing to the Lord their God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Scholarly form of the same harmonization: the command was symbolic, not an actual marriage to a prostitute, so it does not enjoin the act the law forbids.

excerpts.excerpt_text: To marry such a one was not malum in se - evil in itself, but only malum per accidens - incidentally an evil … but not a sin when God commanded it for a holy end; nay, if commanded, it was his duty, and he must trust God with his reputation.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Carries the distinct second harmonization strand: even taken as a real act, marrying such a woman is not intrinsically evil and ceases to be sin when God commands it for a holy end.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament (1861-75), on Hosea 1:2 and 3:1
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this passage directly, arguing the command was of a 'purely symbolical character' that 'did not contemplate an actual and outward marriage,' and so does not enjoin the conduct the law forbids.
